title: Estius: rousing grace actually wakes the sinner
source_text: XL. Igitur per gratiam excitantem intelligunt illam qua homini peccatori, aut a bono opere cessanti, & tanquam quodam sopore depresso, ita immittitur cogitatio, desiderium, & voluntas boni operis, ut jam vere excitatus a somno peccati, aut negligentiae bonorum operum dici possit. Gratiam vero adjuvantem vocant illam qua is qui jam est excitatus adjuvatur, ut perfectius velit quod jam velle incepit: utque perficiat quod jam voluit. Excitat enim, inquiunt, gratia ut velimus, adjuvat ut faciamus. Excitantis gratiae est velle; adjuvantis facere atque perficere. Quae interpretatio est Gulielmi Estii in lib. 2. sentent. distinct. 26. paragr. undecimo.
pass_a_gloss: XL. Therefore by rousing grace they understand that by which to a sinful man, or one ceasing from good work, and as it were weighed down by a certain sleep, thought, desire, and will of a good work is so sent in, that he can now be said to be truly roused from the sleep of sin, or of negligence of good works. But helping grace they call that by which he who is already roused is helped, that he may will more perfectly what he has already begun to will: and that he may complete what he has already willed. For grace, they say, rouses that we may will, helps that we may do. Of rousing grace it is to will; of helping, to do and to perfect. Which interpretation is of William Estius on book 2 of the Sentences distinction 26 paragraph eleven.
pass_b_english: Thesis XL. By rousing grace, then, they mean the grace by which a sinner, or one who has stopped doing good and lies as if sunk in a kind of sleep, is given the thought, desire and will to do a good work, in such a way that he can now be said to be truly roused from the sleep of sin or from neglect of good works.
By assisting grace they mean the grace by which someone already roused is helped to will more perfectly what he has begun to will, and to carry out what he has already willed.

'Grace,' they say, 'rouses us to will and assists us to do. Willing belongs to rousing grace; doing and completing belong to assisting grace.' This is the interpretation of William Estius on book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 26, paragraph 11.
